overview: This five-page confidential file concerns the discovery and preliminary assessment of the Oshirabetsu graphite deposit in Hokkaido in 1948. A despatch from U.S. Political Adviser William J. Sebald forwards a Nippon Times article claiming that the deposit was the world’s second largest after Ceylon’s and a technical memorandum prepared by the Natural Resources Section of General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. The memorandum describes the mine’s location, history, geology, mining methods, estimated reserves, output, stocks, and transportation problems, while cautioning that prospecting remained incomplete and that the Japanese claim about the deposit’s global importance could not yet be verified.

subfiles.title: Despatch forwarding reports on the Oshirabetsu graphite discovery
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards a newspaper article and a SCAP technical memorandum concerning the reported discovery of Japan’s first major graphite deposit.
subfiles.summary: Sebald transmits a Nippon Times article of August 28, 1948, and a memorandum prepared by the Natural Resources Section of General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. He notes that the Japanese Geological Survey reportedly considered the mine the world’s second largest graphite deposit. Officials at headquarters, however, could not verify that claim while survey work remained unfinished.

subfiles.title: Nippon Times article, “Graphite Mine Located”
subfiles.about: The article announces the discovery of a large graphite deposit at Oshirabetsu in Hokkaido and presents official claims about its size.
subfiles.summary: The article reports that a graphite deposit near Hiroo Station in Tokachi Province had been assessed as containing more than 100,000 tons and was claimed to rank second only to Ceylon’s deposit. The site had formerly been worked for nickel and was recognized as a rich graphite deposit in April 1947. It was subsequently developed by the Japan Carbon Company and investigated through physical and electrical prospecting by the Underground Resources Institute; a Sapporo mining official characterized it as exceptionally large.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Record on the Oshirabetsu Graphite Mine
subfiles.from: Hideshiro Hasegawa, Scientific Consultant, Mining and Geology Division, Natural Resources Section
subfiles.about: The memorandum provides a preliminary technical assessment of the Oshirabetsu mine’s location, geology, workings, reserves, production, stocks, and transportation limitations.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on information from Japan Carbon Company and Japanese Geological Survey personnel, the memorandum identifies the ore as crystalline graphite averaging about 26 percent fixed carbon and describes four known lenticular bodies within gabbro. On provisional assumptions, electromagnetic prospecting suggested total reserves of about 160,000 metric tons of ore grading 25–35 percent carbon, although the grade and depth could not be determined by the prospecting methods used. Mining employed open-pit workings and adits, hand tools, blasting, hand sorting, and shipment to a concentrating plant in Toyama Prefecture. Output and stock tables cover March–July 1948, while the report identifies scarce ferry capacity between Hakodate and Aomori and the absence of an on-site flotation plant as the principal obstacles to increased production.

interest: The file is useful for tracing how an optimistic Japanese newspaper announcement was evaluated and qualified by occupation authorities using preliminary geological evidence. Its technical memorandum preserves unusually detailed information about a short-lived postwar mining operation, including ore-body dimensions, carbon grades, extraction methods, monthly output, stocks, and transport routes. It also illustrates the material constraints of postwar Japan: even a potentially important strategic-mineral deposit could not be fully exploited because of limited ferry capacity and the absence of local processing facilities. The conflicting despatch numbers appearing across the pages—617, 618, and No. 610—also provide evidence of the bundle’s administrative transmission and filing history.
